title: The cognitive neuroscience of auditory distraction

findings.antecedent: easy working-memory task (visual presentation of 6 digits, report in order) compared to control task (1-6 in numerical order)
findings.consequent: activation of brain regions (left inferior frontal cortex, left anterior cingulate cortex, left inferior parietal cortex, right precuneus, bilateral anterior insular cortex, left lentiform nucleus, left thalamus, bilateral cerebellum)
findings.mechanism: involvement of this region in working-memory function
findings.quote: This comparison revealed a working-memory effect characterised by an activation of a large-scale network of brain regions.

findings.antecedent: easy working-memory task with changing-state speech sounds compared to steady-state speech sounds
findings.consequent: deactivation of brain regions involved in working memory (left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, bilateral secondary auditory cortex, left inferior parietal cortex)
findings.mechanism: Changing-state material resulted in a suppression of several brain areas, crucially involving left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex and brain regions implicated in the temporary storage of speech-based material
findings.quote: relative to steady-state material, change-of-state caused a deactivation of several of the regions involved in working memory.

findings.antecedent: easy working-memory task with changing-state speech sounds compared to steady-state speech sounds
findings.mechanism: these effects of changing-state sound on the brain were not shown to adversely influence working-memory performance on this task.
findings.quote: these effects of changing-state sound on the brain were not shown to adversely influence working-memory performance on this task.

findings.antecedent: difficult working-memory task (8 digits per list) compared to easy working-memory task (6 digits per list)
findings.consequent: involvement of the right dorsolateral prefrontal 'manipulation' cortex
findings.mechanism: The additional demands of the task recruited the involvement of the dorsolateral prefrontal 'manipulation' cortex on this difficult working-memory task [4].
findings.quote: The additional demands of the task recruited the involvement of the dorsolateral prefrontal 'manipulation' cortex on this difficult working-memory task [4].

findings.antecedent: ignored speech sounds during a difficult working-memory task (8 digits)
findings.quote: ignored speech sounds disrupted working-memory performance [4].

findings.antecedent: changing-state speech sounds during a difficult working-memory task compared to steady-state speech sounds
findings.mechanism: this changing-state effect also activated the dorsolateral prefrontal cortices.
findings.quote: this changing-state effect also activated the dorsolateral prefrontal cortices.

findings.antecedent: higher memory demands of a difficult task AND changing-state sound
findings.mechanism: this distracting sound thus crucially influences the processes of executive functioning within the brain [12,16] that support the active selection, monitoring and manipulation of information in working memory.
findings.quote: similarities between the brain regions activated by working-memory and changing-state effects were confined to the dorsolateral prefrontal 'manipulation' cortex.

findings.antecedent: difficult working-memory task (8 digits) compared to easy working-memory task (6 digits)
findings.mechanism: The 10% decrease in baseline performance (6 digits: 93% correct, compared with 8 digits: 83% correct) on this more difficult task might be one of the reasons why this task was more susceptible to disruption.
findings.quote: The 10% decrease in baseline performance (6 digits: 93% correct, compared with 8 digits: 83% correct) on this more difficult task might be one of the reasons why this task was more susceptible to disruption.

findings.antecedent: difficult working-memory task with ignored speech disrupting performance
findings.quote: Indeed, on the difficult task, when ignored speech disrupted working-memory performance [4], this physiological suppression was not apparent.

stimuli.description: steady-state (e.g., AAA...) and changing-state (e.g., ABAB...) speech sounds
lists of 6 or 8 digits presented visually

limitations: It remains an open question whether disruption of working memory by auditory distraction on tasks with low memory demands is related to the absence of suppression or the activation of some additional brain mechanism.

It remains an open question whether the involvement of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is crucial to the disruption of working-memory performance when the content of the to-be-remembered material is visual-spatial.
